beats.say: Every thread does its own work, with a live checklist you can watch.
When you run out of tokens, the whole project pauses.

beats.big: Or picks up in another tool.
beats.say: Or the work moves to a completely different tool. Let me show you how.

lines: Edit built in a Claude Code project
beats.say: But first, a quick heads-up: that's not really me. This is my AI avatar, speaking with my cloned voice. The face, the voice, the edit and the captions were all made with AI, from instructions I gave inside a Claude Code project. I want you to see what's actually possible today. So let's get into it.
Claude Code Projects and Opus 5.5: a full demo, with real screens and real output.
First, the recent releases.

beats.say: And fourth, GPT 6 Sol. It shipped the same day as Opus 5.5, and for me it was the disappointment of the month. In my side-by-side tests, it just didn't hold up.
Chapter two: Opus 5.5 inside Claude Code.
Let's start with the model. On my account, Opus 5.5 is now the default in Claude Code.
Click the model name and the picker opens, with Opus 5.5 ticked right at the top.
Below it are Fable 5.1, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 4.5, each with its own number key.
Right next to it is effort. Faster on the left, smarter on the right.
Medium is the recommended default. I turn it up for planning and code reviews, and leave it at the default for routine work.
And here's the part I like most. The model is set per thread, not per account.
This thread runs Opus 5.5 at high effort, set right in its own composer, while the project chat next to it runs a different model.
Chapter three. So, what are Projects?
Projects sit right at the top of Claude Code, and each active project shows a live status.
Needs input: a thread is waiting on you.
Ready for review: the work is done and needs your okay.
And working: a thread is running right now.
Here's my full list.
Six products, six projects. Each one is private, pinned in the sidebar, and keeps its own history, threads and memory.
Creating a new one has just three fields, and only the name is required.
A name.
A goal, which is optional.
And context: the repositories the project works in.
Chapter four. Let me show you a real one.
This is EasyChamp, my sports platform, running as a Claude Code project.
On the left is the project chat. You talk to one coordinator here, like you would to a teammate.
On the right is every thread it started. Each one is its own agent session, with its own context.
Eighteen threads are waiting on me right now,
and fifty-two are idle: finished, parked, or waiting on a decision inside the thread.
Now watch what the coordinator does with a message.
I asked how a match page was built and what it costs, and it spun up a thread just for that question, with its own scope.
It even splits threads. The TikTok question was pulled out of the tracking thread into a thread of its own.
Open any thread, and it's a full agent session.
There's a live checklist: read the handoff notes, audit the commands, sweep two hundred twenty-four checkouts, and push the index.
Threads also get messages from the coordinator. This one received seven.
And then there's the wall every heavy user hits: usage limit reached.
So here's what I asked the coordinator.
In short: get every thread ready for a handoff, so the work can keep going in another tool or subscription.
And it started a handoff readiness thread for exactly that. One ask, one thread.
Chapter five: what keeps a project moving.
Routines are agents that run on a schedule or on a trigger. Here are the built-in templates.
A morning briefing, email triage, a system health check, issue triage.
Pull request digests, dependency checks, and release notes every time something merges.
And here's what happens when you hit the weekly limit.
The whole project pauses, and Claude tells you exactly when it will pick everything back up on its own.
Auto-continue restarts every thread once the limit resets.
That helps. But you can't always wait for a reset. So what if you need to keep going right now?
Chapter six. You hand off.
This is SpecWeave, my open-source tool. It keeps the work itself in git: the spec, the tasks, who's on what, and the next step. I've set it to hand off by itself at ninety percent of the limit.
When I'm close to the limit, I just say hand off, or it fires on its own. It releases my task, writes down where things stand, and pushes my branch, including uncommitted edits.
Then in another tool, on another machine or account, I say: pick up.
And it comes back with the same spec, the same task, the next step and its acceptance criteria. Right where I left off.
It's free. To install it, run N P M install, dash G, specweave. The command is in the description.

That's Claude Code Projects with Opus 5.5. One coordinator, many threads, each one a real agent session. And when you run out of usage, you hand off and keep going. The links are in the description. And once more: this was my AI avatar. The real me set all of this up and reviewed it before it went live. See you in the next one.
